newsitem.title: JAPAN: Little JGB impact seen from Nomura suspension.
newsitem.headline: Little JGB impact seen from Nomura suspension.

text.p: Nomura Securities Co Ltd has been dealt a blow by the Japanese Ministry of Finance's (MOF) suspension of it from its lucrative bond underwriting business, but the impact on the bond market may be limited, analysts and bond traders said on Wednesday.
MOF announced on Tuesday that it was suspending Nomura from Japanese government bond (JGB) auctions and underwriting until administrative penalties against the brokerage are implemented.

"We cannot say there will be no impact, but the bond market to a certain extent had already factored in the likelihood of Nomura being shut out of JGB auctions," said a manager at a major brokerage house.
A MOF official briefing reporters on Tuesday said that Nomura currently had a 5.98 percent share in JGB underwriting, the biggest among underwriting syndicate members.
Six city banks were in second place, each holding a 3.29 percent share, the official said.

"There is unlikely to be a strong impact on the JGB market from Nomura's suspension. There are a plenty of other brokerage houses," said Kazuhiko Sano, manager and chief strategist at Sumitomo Capital Securities.
The MOF official said the ministry would consult with the underwriting syndicate to arrange for other underwriters to fill in Nomura's share.

Suspension is expected to harm Nomura's profitability and prestige but the firm is likely to be able to carry out its bond business by dealing through other brokerage houses, analysts and traders said.

"Nomura will still be able to buy JGBs from the secondary market and it can also use its brokerage allies to bid at auctions if it wants to. So I don't see why this should pose a disaster for JGBs," said a senior trader at a European brokerage firm.
Some bond traders were less optimistic, saying Nomura had a huge client base and some smaller institutional investors had bond accounts only at Nomura.

"We may see some negative impact, especially in the corporate bond market (after administrative penalties are implemented). Nomura's market-making power is quite enormous," said a bond trader at a second-tier brokerage house.
The Tokyo metropolitan government and the Yokohama city government said on Wednesday they are considering removing Nomura from bond underwriting.
The Postal Savings Bureau (Yucho) and the Postal Life Insurance Bureau (Kampo) of the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications said on Wednesday they have halted securities business with Nomura.
A ministry official said Yucho's suspension of securities business with Nomura includes JGB repo transactions.
An official at Nomura said Kampo had already stopped repo transactions with the brokerage.
Kampo, one of the world's biggest investors, holds an enormous pool of funds that amounted to 97.2182 trillion yen as of end of February. It is also a major bond lender in the JGB repo market.
Yucho, the largest bond lender in the JGB repo market, is also among the largest investors with net assets of 35.2132 trillion yen as of the end of March 1996.
Bond traders said the moves by Yucho and Kampo were unlikely to have a serious impact on the JGB repo market.
"More players are starting to participate in the repo market as bond lenders. So we are not expecting Nomura's problems to result in a sharp rise in repo rates," said a brokerage house trader.

In the JGB repo market, JGBs are borrowed or loaned with cash as collateral. The outstanding balance of the market at the end of March stood at 17.0371 trillion yen, up from 12.8230 trillion yen in February, according to the Japan Securities Dealers' Association.
